title: The Queen of Heaven in Egypt
summary: In Jeremiah's last recorded message, God confronts the Judeans living throughout Egypt for burning incense to other gods, the very sin that brought Jerusalem to ruin. The people, led by the women with their husbands' approval, answer that life went well when they worshiped the Queen of Heaven and badly when they stopped, and they vow to continue. Jeremiah replies that the disaster came because of that worship, and he gives a sign: Pharaoh Hophra will fall to his enemies as Zedekiah fell to Nebuchadnezzar.
story: This is the last scene of Jeremiah's ministry the book records, and it is a sad one. The prophet who began under Josiah now speaks to a scattered community in Egypt that has learned nothing from the fall of Jerusalem. The chapter mirrors Jeremiah's temple sermon of chapter 7, where he had already condemned families for baking cakes to the Queen of Heaven (7:18). Forty years later, after the destruction he predicted, the same practice continues in a foreign land. The people's reply is the clearest statement anywhere in the book of an alternative reading of history, and Jeremiah's answer is his final word on it. After this the book turns to a personal word to Baruch (chapter 45) and then to the oracles against the nations.
historical:
Verse 1 names Judean communities across Egypt: Migdol and Tahpanhes in the eastern Nile Delta, Memphis (the old capital near modern Cairo), and Pathros, the Hebrew name for Upper Egypt in the south. The spread suggests that Judean settlement in Egypt had grown beyond the group that came with Johanan, and that some had arrived earlier. A century and more later, Aramaic papyri from the island of Elephantine in southern Egypt document a Jewish military colony there with its own temple to the God of Israel. Some of those papyri mention other deities alongside him, a mix of worship that resembles what this chapter describes. Scholars do not know whether that colony descended from Jeremiah's hearers.

The people's claim in verses 17 and 18 is often read against the reforms of King Josiah, who about 622 BC removed the shrines of other gods (2 Kings 23). After that, Josiah was killed in battle at Megiddo in 609 BC, Judah became subject first to Egypt and then to Babylon, and Jerusalem was destroyed. From their point of view, abandoning the Queen of Heaven had brought disaster. Pharaoh Hophra (Apries), named in verse 30, was overthrown in about 570 BC by his general Amasis after a military revolt. The Greek historian Herodotus reports that Apries was later killed by Egyptians hostile to him.
cultural:
The Queen of Heaven was a goddess whose worship was popular in Judah, especially in households. Scholars identify her with various goddesses of the region: the Mesopotamian Ishtar, whose symbol was the morning and evening star; the Canaanite Astarte; or perhaps Asherah or Anat. The worship involved families working together: in 7:18 the children gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead dough for cakes. Here the women bake cakes made in her image (verse 19), perhaps molded in the shape of the goddess or her star. Clay molds and figurines of female figures have been found at many Judean sites of this period, though their exact use is debated.

The women's appeal to their husbands' knowledge in verse 19 reflects the law of vows in Numbers 30, where a husband could annul a vow his wife made. By saying their husbands knew, the women were claiming their vows were valid and binding. Drink offerings, poured out as a gift to a deity, were part of worship across the ancient world, including Israel's own sacrifices (Numbers 15:5).
literary: The chapter is built as a formal dispute in three rounds. God's accusation (verses 1 to 14) reviews the history of Judah's idolatry and warns the Egyptian community. The people's reply (verses 15 to 19) is blunt: "we will not listen to you" (verse 16). Jeremiah's response (verses 20 to 30) reinterprets their history and ends with a sign. The key word is the verb to stand (verses 25, 28, 29): the people want their vows to stand, and God says the question is "whose word will stand, Mine or theirs" (verse 28). Jeremiah's sarcastic command in verse 25, "Keep your vows", leaves them to the choice they have made. The repeated phrase "in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem" ties Egypt's sin to the sin that destroyed the homeland.

outline.t: Why repeat the same sin in Egypt?
Judgment on the remnant in Egypt
The people's reply: we will serve the Queen of Heaven
Jeremiah: that worship is why disaster came
Keep your vows, and the sign of Pharaoh Hophra

doctrines.note: The chapter shows idolatry as a stubborn habit of the heart that survives even catastrophe. The people interpret their suffering as proof that they need more idolatry, not less.

The dispute is finally about whose reading of history is true: the people's, based on their experience of prosperity, or God's, given through his prophets. God's word is the interpreter of events, not the other way around.
God lets the people have what they insist on (verse 25), which is itself a form of judgment. Yet he promises that a few will escape and return (verse 28), so even here judgment is not total.

words.note: Melekhet, queen, used in the title Queen of Heaven (verses 17 to 19, 25). The Hebrew is unusual, and the vowels in the traditional text may have been adjusted to read work (as in work of heaven) instead of queen, perhaps to avoid giving the goddess a royal title. Most translations read queen.

Kavvan, a cake or bun used in worship. It appears only here and in 7:18 in the Hebrew Bible, both times for the Queen of Heaven. The word may be borrowed from Akkadian, the language of Mesopotamia, where a similar word names cakes offered to Ishtar.

Neder, a vow. A vow was a solemn promise to a deity, often to give something in return for help. The people insist on keeping their vows to the Queen of Heaven (verse 25), while they had broken their oath to obey the LORD (42:5-6).

Qatar, to burn incense or make an offering go up in smoke. It is the chapter's most repeated verb, used ten times from verse 3 onward. Burning incense was a normal part of worship, but here it stands for worship of other gods.

christ: The people read their history and concluded that serving the Queen of Heaven had kept them safe. Jeremiah insists that only God's word can interpret history truly. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who interprets Israel's whole story, explaining to his disciples after his resurrection how all the Scriptures pointed to him (Luke 24:27). The link here is thematic rather than predictive: the chapter shows a people unable to read their suffering rightly, and the gospel presents the cross, the moment that looked like the ultimate disaster, as the place where God's purpose was most fully revealed. The promise of a few who would escape and return also belongs to the Old Testament theme of the remnant, which the New Testament picks up in speaking of the people God preserves by grace (Romans 11:5).

hard.q: The women's argument seems to be based on real experience: things were better when they worshiped the Queen of Heaven. How should a reader weigh it?
hard.a: The argument is not foolish, and the chapter lets it be heard in the people's own words. Life under Manasseh, who promoted other gods, was relatively stable, while the years after Josiah's reform brought his death, foreign domination, and destruction. Jeremiah's reply is that they have read the timeline too narrowly: the judgment fell because of generations of accumulated sin, including the long years of idolatry before Josiah, and Josiah's reform, though sincere, did not change the heart of the nation (3:10). 2 Kings 23:26 makes the same point, that the LORD did not turn from his anger because of what Manasseh had done. The chapter doesn't pretend that faithfulness always brings immediate prosperity. Its claim is that God's word, not short-term outcomes, is the right measure of truth, a claim that asks for faith in the face of evidence that seems to point the other way.

questions: The people interpreted their suffering as proof that they should return to their old gods. How do we tend to read events in a way that confirms what we already want to believe?
The women argued from experience, and Jeremiah argued from God's word. When experience and Scripture seem to point in different directions, how do you decide which to trust?
God tells the people to go ahead and keep their vows. What does it mean that sometimes the judgment is simply being given what we insist on?
